summary:
San Marino does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Homosexual acts were decriminalised in 1864, and the residual Article 274 of the Criminal Code, which punished 'habitual' homosexual acts causing public scandal with three months to one year of imprisonment, was repealed in September 2004 and was never reported as applied. No provision of San Marino law penalises gender identity, and no statute regulates which bathrooms or facilities a person may use.

Entry carries no documented friction. The border with Italy is open, and no recorded identity screening procedure risks outing an arriving visitor.

Legal gender recognition does not exist. The 2026 edition of the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map lists San Marino among the countries with no functioning legal or administrative process for changing a gender marker. The practical consequence falls on residents rather than travellers: a visitor's foreign documents govern throughout a stay, and no domestic procedure exists that could alter them.

Protection machinery is keyed to sexual orientation rather than gender identity. A referendum of 2 June 2019, passed with 71.46% in favour, added a prohibition of discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation to Article 4 of the Declaration of Citizens' Rights; the Grand and General Council vote in March 2019 had fallen short at 35 for, 8 against and 1 abstention, short of the 39 required. Since 3 May 2008 the Penal Code has outlawed discrimination and hate speech based on sexual orientation and provides penalty enhancements for hate crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation. In November 2019 San Marino accepted Universal Periodic Review recommendations to outlaw discrimination based on gender identity; whether that acceptance has been enacted is not sourced here.

There are occasionally reports of violence and hate crimes against the LGBTQ community in San Marino. No trans-specific pattern of violence is documented in the sources, and none is recorded as state-tolerated.

Relationship recognition is available but stops short of marriage. Civil unions entered into force on 5 December 2018 and became fully operational on 11 February 2019, granting couples rights over residency and citizenship, pensions, healthcare, succession and stepchild adoption. Same-sex couples remain barred from marrying, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex couples. A December 2017 budget-law amendment allowed foreign same-sex couples to marry in San Marino to encourage tourism, but as of 2024 the implementing legislation does not appear to have been drafted.

The age of consent is 14 for both opposite-sex and same-sex sexual acts, and inciting a minor under 18 to sexual corruption is an offence. Gay and bisexual men are permitted to donate blood.
tangentialFactors:
San Marino's official climate is markedly more permissive than its thin statutory record suggests. In April 2022 Paolo Rondelli was appointed captain regent, a six-month ceremonial post without executive power, making San Marino the first country in modern history with an openly gay head of state.

San Marino was one of 12 countries examined at the 34th session of the Universal Periodic Review Working Group in November 2019, and it accepted the SOGIESC recommendations put to it at that review, including the recommendation to outlaw discrimination based on gender identity.

Public discussion of LGBTQ matters has historically been muted. Until recently LGBTQ people in San Marino went unnoticed, with very few public debates in media, society or politics, and in the early 2000s the government rejected LGBTQ groups' request to recognise 17 May as the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia.

The gap between civil union and marriage is the principal structural inequality: same-sex couples hold residency, citizenship, pension, healthcare, succession and stepchild-adoption rights through civil union, but no custody-specific provisions beyond stepchild adoption are recorded, and full marital status remains unavailable.
localsOnly:
Residents live under a constitutional-level non-discrimination clause on sexual orientation, adopted by referendum in June 2019 after the legislature's own vote failed to reach the required threshold, alongside a Penal Code offence of discrimination and hate speech in force since 3 May 2008 with hate-crime penalty enhancements.

Civil unions, fully operational since 11 February 2019, carry residency and citizenship consequences for Sammarinese couples as well as pension, healthcare, succession and stepchild-adoption rights.

San Marino's sex education programme, together with its emotional education programmes, expressly provides for knowledge of LGBTQ rights, and the Curriculum of Education to Citizenship also covers LGBTQ matters.

Gay and bisexual men are allowed to donate blood, and the age of consent is set at 14 irrespective of the sexes involved.
outOfScopeNotes:
The ILGA Annual Review 2026 chapter on legal gender recognition does not carry a San Marino entry; the documented cases in that chapter concern Albania and Andorra. The San Marino finding rests on the 2026 Rainbow Map listing alone.

Whether the gender-identity discrimination prohibition accepted at the November 2019 Universal Periodic Review has since been written into San Marino statute is unresolved in the sources consulted.

The Guardian dates legal recognition of gay couples in San Marino to 2016, while the civil-union statute was approved in November 2018 and entered into force in December 2018. The discrepancy is unresolved here.

Whether the Penal Code's hate-crime penalty enhancements extend to offences motivated by the victim's gender identity, as opposed to sexual orientation, is not sourced.

No trans-specific violence statistics or case outcomes are available for San Marino; the sources record only occasional reports of violence and hate crimes against the LGBTQ community in general.

Whether the December 2017 amendment permitting foreign same-sex couples to marry has acquired implementing legislation after 2024 is unresolved.
